q: What colour are the reflective studs (cat's eyes) between the hard shoulder and the left-hand running lane of a motorway?
explanation: RED studs mark the left-hand edge of the carriageway next to the hard shoulder or verge. Think: 'Red = edge of road / boundary'.

q: Where will you find GREEN reflective studs on a motorway or dual carriageway?
options: At slip road entries and exits
explanation: GREEN studs mark deceleration and acceleration lanes at slip road entries and exits.

q: What colour are the reflective studs adjacent to the central reservation on a motorway?
explanation: AMBER studs mark the right-hand edge of the carriageway next to the central reservation.

q: What do fluorescent green/yellow reflective studs indicate on a motorway or dual carriageway?
options: Temporary lane markings at roadworks or contraflow systems
A dedicated bus or HGV lane
explanation: Fluorescent bright green/yellow studs indicate temporary lane layouts and contraflow systems during roadworks.

q: What colour are the reflective studs between individual running traffic lanes on a motorway?
explanation: WHITE studs separate lanes of traffic travelling in the same direction.

q: On a Smart Motorway, what does a red 'X' displayed on an overhead gantry above your lane mean?
options: The lane is closed; you MUST move out of this lane immediately
Overtaking is permitted if the road ahead is clear
explanation: A red 'X' means the lane is closed. It is strictly illegal to drive in a lane showing a red 'X' (subject to a £100 fine and 3 penalty points).

q: If you break down in an Emergency Area (EA) on a Smart Motorway, what should you do when using the emergency roadside telephone?
options: Face oncoming traffic so you can see approaching danger
Turn your back to the road to hear better
Wait inside the car until the operator answers
Walk to the next junction to meet the recovery vehicle
explanation: Always face oncoming traffic when using a roadside emergency phone so you can see any approaching danger or errant vehicles.

q: Which vehicle is prohibited from using the outside (right-hand) lane of a motorway with three or more lanes?
options: A car towing a caravan or trailer
An electric car with four passengers
explanation: Any vehicle towing a trailer or caravan, and goods vehicles exceeding 7.5 tonnes, are prohibited from using the right-hand lane of a motorway with 3 or more lanes.

q: Approximately how far apart are Emergency Refuge Areas (ERAs) spaced on All Lane Running (ALR) Smart Motorways?
explanation: Emergency Areas on Smart Motorways are located approximately every 1 to 1.5 miles, marked by large blue signs with an orange SOS phone symbol.

q: Why is an emergency telephone on a motorway preferable to using a personal mobile phone?
options: It connects directly to the regional control centre and automatically provides your exact location
It is free of charge while mobile roaming costs apply
It has a built-in satellite loudspeaker
Police cannot track mobile phone calls on motorways
explanation: Motorway SOS phones connect directly to National Highways and automatically pin your exact location and carriageway direction.

q: What is the total dry stopping distance (thinking + braking) at 30 mph according to the Highway Code?
explanation: At 30 mph: Thinking = 9m (30ft), Braking = 14m (45ft). Total = 23 metres (75 feet), or about 6 car lengths.

q: What is the total dry stopping distance at 50 mph?
explanation: At 50 mph: Thinking = 15m (50ft), Braking = 38m (125ft). Total = 53 metres (175 feet), or 13 car lengths.

q: What is the total dry stopping distance at 70 mph?
explanation: At 70 mph: Thinking = 21m (70ft), Braking = 75m (245ft). Total = 96 metres (315 feet), or 24 car lengths.

q: What is the total dry stopping distance at 20 mph?
explanation: At 20 mph: Thinking = 6m (20ft), Braking = 6m (20ft). Total = 12 metres (40 feet), or 3 car lengths.

q: What is the total dry stopping distance at 60 mph?
explanation: At 60 mph: Thinking = 18m (60ft), Braking = 55m (180ft). Total = 73 metres (240 feet), or 18 car lengths.

q: In wet weather, by how much does your total stopping distance increase?
options: It remains identical if tyres have 3mm tread
explanation: Wet roads reduce tyre grip and at least DOUBLE (x2) your stopping distance. Maintain a 4-second gap.

q: In icy or snowy conditions, by how much can your stopping distance increase?
explanation: On ice and hard-packed snow, stopping distances can increase by up to TEN TIMES (x10). Drive in the highest gear possible to avoid wheelspin.

q: What is the fast mental shortcut to calculate Thinking Distance in feet for any speed in dry conditions?
options: Thinking distance in feet is always exactly equal to your speed in mph (e.g. 50 mph = 50 ft)
explanation: In feet, Thinking Distance ALWAYS equals your speed in mph: 20mph = 20ft, 30mph = 30ft, 40mph = 40ft, 50mph = 50ft, 60mph = 60ft, 70mph = 70ft!

q: In dry conditions, what is the minimum safe following distance between you and the vehicle in front?
options: One car length for every 5 mph
explanation: Use the 2-second rule in dry conditions ('Only a fool breaks the two-second rule'). Double it to 4 seconds in the wet.

q: If streetlights are present on a road with no speed limit signs posted, what is the default speed limit?
explanation: The presence of a system of street lighting indicates a 30 mph speed limit in England, Scotland & NI (20 mph in Wales), unless signs indicate otherwise.

q: What is the national speed limit on a SINGLE carriageway road for a car-derived van (<2 tonnes max laden weight)?
explanation: Car-derived vans (under 2 tonnes maximum laden weight) have the same speed limits as normal cars: 60 mph on single carriageways and 70 mph on dual carriageways.

q: What is the national speed limit on a SINGLE carriageway road for a standard panel van (such as a Ford Transit)?
explanation: Standard goods vans (not car-derived) are subject to lower limits: 50 mph on single carriageways and 60 mph on dual carriageways!

q: What is the maximum speed limit for a car towing a caravan or trailer on a motorway?
explanation: When towing a caravan or trailer, the maximum speed limit on a motorway or dual carriageway is 60 mph (50 mph on single carriageways).

q: What is the maximum speed limit for a car towing a trailer on a DUAL carriageway?
explanation: A car towing a trailer is limited to 60 mph on dual carriageways (reduced from the normal 70 mph limit).

q: What is the speed limit on a single carriageway road for an articulated goods vehicle over 7.5 tonnes in England and Wales?
explanation: In England and Wales, the speed limit for HGVs over 7.5 tonnes on single carriageways is 50 mph (in Scotland it remains 40 mph unless dual carriageway).

q: At a PELICAN crossing, what does a FLASHING AMBER light mean?
options: You MUST give way to pedestrians already on the crossing; proceed if clear
Stop and wait for the green light
explanation: At a Pelican crossing, FLASHING AMBER means give way to pedestrians on the crossing. If the crossing is clear, you may proceed without waiting for green.

q: How does a PUFFIN crossing differ from a Pelican crossing?
options: Puffin has infrared/heat sensors and NO flashing amber phase; it uses standard light sequence
Puffin has flashing amber for 10 seconds
Puffin is exclusively for horse riders
Puffin requires you to sound your horn before proceeding
explanation: PUFFIN (Pedestrian User-Friendly INtelligent) crossings have electronic sensors to detect pedestrians. They do NOT have a flashing amber phase.

q: What distinguishes a TOUCAN crossing from other pedestrian crossings?
options: Cyclists and pedestrians can cross together without dismounting
It is only operated during school hours
It has twin flashing red lights
Only two pedestrians are permitted to cross at a time
explanation: TOUCAN ('Two-Can') crossings are wide crossings designed for pedestrians AND cyclists to cross simultaneously without dismounting.

q: What is a PEGASUS crossing designed for?
options: Horse riders (equestrians) with high-mounted push buttons
explanation: PEGASUS crossings are designed for horse riders and pedestrians, featuring push buttons mounted higher up on posts so equestrians do not need to dismount.

q: What are the white zig-zag lines painted on the road approaching a pedestrian crossing for?
options: Strictly prohibit parking AND overtaking the lead vehicle nearest the crossing
Indicate a speed limit reduction to 20 mph
Mark areas where loading is allowed for up to 20 minutes
explanation: White zig-zag lines strictly prohibit both parking/waiting and overtaking the leading vehicle moving or stationary nearest the crossing.

q: At a ZEBRA crossing, when are you legally obligated to stop for a pedestrian?
options: As soon as the pedestrian steps onto the crossing
When they are standing on the pavement looking at you
Only if an amber beacon is flashing
Only if escorted by a school crossing patrol
explanation: You MUST give way once a pedestrian has stepped onto a zebra crossing. However, good practice dictates you should anticipate and stop if someone is waiting.

q: What light signal indicates that a tram route is clear to proceed?
options: A vertical white line on a black background
explanation: Tram signals use white lights on a black background: a vertical white bar means PROCEED; a horizontal white bar means STOP.

q: At an automatic railway level crossing, what do alternating flashing twin red lights mean?
options: You MUST stop behind the stop line
Give way to oncoming road traffic
explanation: Twin alternating flashing red lights mean you MUST STOP. A train is approaching and barriers are lowering. An audible alarm also sounds.

q: What is the legal minimum tyre tread depth for passenger cars in the UK?
options: 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters and around entire circumference
1.0 mm across the entire tyre face
1.6 mm across half the tyre breadth
explanation: Tyres must have a minimum tread depth of 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the breadth of the tyre and around the entire continuous circumference.

q: What is the legal alcohol limit for drivers in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland?
options: 35 mcg breath / 80 mg blood / 107 mg urine
22 mcg breath / 50 mg blood / 67 mg urine
50 mcg breath / 100 mg blood / 120 mg urine
explanation: In England, Wales & NI: 35 micrograms of alcohol per 100ml of breath, 80 milligrams per 100ml of blood, or 107 milligrams per 100ml of urine.

q: What is the legal breath alcohol limit for drivers in SCOTLAND?
explanation: Scotland has a lower, stricter limit: 22 micrograms of alcohol per 100ml of breath (and 50 mg per 100ml of blood).

q: Under the New Drivers Act, how many penalty points within two years of passing your practical test will result in licence revocation?
explanation: Accumulating 6 or more penalty points within 2 years of passing your first practical test automatically revokes your licence. You must re-apply for a provisional and retake BOTH tests.

q: If you are involved in a collision causing injury or damage and cannot exchange details at the scene, within what time must you report it to the police?
options: As soon as reasonably practicable and within 24 hours
explanation: You MUST report the collision to the police in person as soon as reasonably practicable and in any case within 24 hours.

q: If asked by a police officer to produce your driving licence, insurance, or MOT certificate, how long do you have to present them at a police station?
explanation: Under the HO/RT1 procedure, you have 7 days to produce your documents at a police station of your choice.

q: When does a newly registered brand-new car require its very first MOT test?
options: When it reaches 3 years old (then annually)
explanation: New cars require their first MOT test when they reach 3 years old from registration, and every year thereafter.

q: How long does a Statutory Off Road Notification (SORN) remain valid?
options: Indefinitely until the vehicle is taxed, sold, exported, or scrapped
explanation: A SORN declaration now remains valid indefinitely until the vehicle is re-taxed, sold, permanently exported, or broken up/scrapped.

q: Between what hours is it illegal to sound your car horn in a built-up area (unless avoiding an immediate danger)?
explanation: The horn curfew in built-up areas is 11:30 pm to 7:00 am. It is also illegal to sound the horn when stationary unless another vehicle poses danger.

q: What legal requirements must a passenger meet to supervise a learner driver holding a provisional licence?
options: Be at least 21 years old and have held a full car licence for at least 3 years
Be at least 18 years old and held a licence for 1 year
Be at least 25 years old with no penalty points
Be an immediate family member of any age
explanation: A supervising driver must be at least 21 years of age and have held a full licence for the vehicle category for at least 3 years.

q: When parking at night on a road with a speed limit greater than 30 mph, what MUST you do?
options: Leave your parking lights (sidelights) on and park facing the direction of traffic
Leave your hazard warning lights flashing
Park on the pavement to keep the road clear
Switch off all lights to preserve battery
explanation: On roads where the speed limit is above 30 mph, you MUST leave parking lights on at night and park facing the direction of traffic on the left.

q: What does a circular blue sign containing a red border and a single red diagonal stripe mean?
options: Waiting restrictions apply (No Waiting during times shown)
explanation: A single red diagonal bar across a blue circle means NO WAITING during the operational times on the sign. (A full red cross 'X' means Clearway: No Stopping at all).

q: What does a circular sign with a red cross 'X' on a blue background (Clearway sign) mean?
options: No Stopping at any time (even to pick up or set down passengers)
explanation: The red cross on a blue background indicates a Clearway: NO STOPPING under any circumstances, even momentarily to drop off passengers.

q: What does a blue rectangular sign showing a large white arrow pointing UP and a smaller red arrow pointing DOWN mean?
options: You have priority over oncoming vehicles
Oncoming vehicles have priority over you
explanation: The blue rectangle with a large white up-arrow means YOU have priority over oncoming traffic. (A white circle with a red ring and red up-arrow means ONCOMING traffic has priority).

q: What does an empty white circular sign with only a RED border (no symbols inside) mean?
options: No vehicles of any kind permitted (including non-motor vehicles like bicycles)
explanation: A completely blank white circle inside a red ring means 'No Vehicles' — this bans ALL vehicles, including bicycles and horse-drawn carriages.

q: What does a solid blue circular sign showing the number '30' in white text indicate?
options: Minimum mandatory speed limit of 30 mph
Maximum advisory speed limit of 30 mph
explanation: Circular blue signs give mandatory positive orders: a blue circle with '30' is a MINIMUM speed limit of 30 mph.

q: What do TWO yellow stripes painted vertically on the kerbstone indicate?
options: No loading or unloading at ANY time
Loading permitted for up to 20 minutes
explanation: Two yellow kerb marks mean NO LOADING OR UNLOADING AT ANY TIME. (One yellow mark means loading prohibited during times shown on the accompanying plate).

q: Under what circumstance may you legally enter a yellow criss-cross Box Junction and wait?
options: When you want to turn right and are only prevented from doing so by oncoming traffic or right-turning vehicles
When your exit road is blocked by stationary traffic
When entering behind an emergency vehicle
explanation: You MUST NOT enter a box junction unless your exit road is clear, EXCEPT when you wish to turn right and are only prevented from doing so by oncoming traffic or other right-turning vehicles.

q: What does a triangular warning sign displaying an old steam locomotive indicate?
options: Railway level crossing WITHOUT a gate or barrier
Railway level crossing WITH a gate or barrier
explanation: A sign showing a steam train warns of a level crossing WITHOUT a gate or barrier. (A gate/fence illustration warns of a crossing WITH gates or barriers).

q: What do diagonal stripes or chevron markings bordered by a SOLID continuous white line mean?
options: You MUST NOT enter the area except in an emergency
You may enter if it is safe to do so
Only buses and taxis may enter
explanation: If the chevron/hatched area is bounded by a SOLID white line, you MUST NOT enter it except in an emergency. If bordered by broken lines, you should not enter unless safe.

q: What should you do if your caravan or trailer begins to 'snake' (sway violently from side to side)?
options: Ease off the accelerator smoothly and keep the steering wheel steady
Brake hard immediately to bring the outfit to a halt
Accelerate hard to pull the outfit straight
Counter-steer vigorously in rhythm with the sway
explanation: If snaking occurs, ease gently off the accelerator and hold the steering straight. NEVER brake hard or counter-steer, as this will induce a rollover or jack-knife!

q: What is the primary function of a breakaway cable on a braked trailer?
options: To automatically apply the trailer's brakes if it detaches from the towball
To keep electrical lights connected if the hitch fails
To keep the trailer physically attached to the vehicle
explanation: A breakaway cable is a steel safety line connected to the trailer's handbrake. If the trailer unhitches, the cable pulls and locks the trailer brakes before snapping.

q: Why is it dangerous and prohibited to bump-start or push-start a modern petrol car fitted with a catalytic converter?
options: Unburnt fuel can enter the exhaust system and damage or ignite the catalytic converter
It will blow the ABS electronic fuse
It causes engine timing belt slippage
It burns out the alternator diodes
explanation: Push-starting causes unburnt fuel to flow into the hot exhaust and catalytic converter, leading to overheating, melting, or permanent damage.

q: What is the correct procedure to clear a clogged Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) warning light?
options: Drive at a sustained speed of 40-50+ mph on an open road for 20-30 minutes
Idle the engine at high revs while stationary for 10 minutes
Pour cold water over the exhaust silencer
Disconnect and reconnect the 12V battery terminal
explanation: A DPF requires high exhaust temperatures to burn off accumulated soot ('active regeneration'). Drive at sustained speeds (e.g. on a motorway or dual carriageway) for 20 to 30 minutes.

q: What is the maximum legal width for any trailer or caravan towed by a passenger car in the UK?
explanation: The maximum permitted width for any trailer towed by a car (gross weight up to 3,500 kg) is 2.55 metres. Max length (excluding towbar) is 7.0 metres.

q: When should tyre pressures always be checked with an accurate pressure gauge?
options: Immediately after a long fast motorway journey
Only when the tyre looks visibly deflated
Only when the ambient temperature is above 20°C
explanation: Tyre pressures must be checked when tyres are COLD. Friction from driving heats the air inside tyres, causing expansion and artificially high pressure readings.

q: What handling symptom occurs if one of your car's FRONT tyres suffers a sudden high-speed blowout?
options: The steering wheel will pull violently towards the side of the blown tyre
The rear end will fishtail from side to side
The brake pedal will drop straight to the floor
The engine will immediately cut out
explanation: A front tyre blowout creates severe drag on that side, pulling the steering wheel heavily towards the blown tyre. Grip the wheel firmly and ease off the accelerator.

q: What is 'brake fade' and what is the primary cause?
options: A loss of braking effectiveness caused by pads/discs overheating on long downhill gradients
Air trapped in the brake fluid reservoir
Water entering the brake master cylinder
explanation: Brake fade is when friction surfaces overheat from continuous braking, drastically reducing stopping power. Prevent it by selecting a lower gear (engine braking) on descents.

q: How does Anti-Lock Braking (ABS) assist a driver during an emergency stop?
options: It prevents wheels from locking, allowing you to maintain steering control while braking heavily
It automatically shortens braking distance in all road conditions
It detects obstacles ahead using radar and applies brakes automatically
It prevents tyre blowouts by reducing brake pressure
explanation: ABS prevents wheels from locking up, which allows you to steer around obstacles even while pressing the brake pedal as hard as possible. You should NOT pump the pedal.

q: In emergency first aid, what does the 'DR ABC' protocol stand for?
explanation: DR ABC: Danger (ensure the scene is safe), Response (check if casualty is conscious), Airway (tilt head, lift chin), Breathing (check for up to 10s), Circulation (control major bleeding).

q: When performing adult CPR chest compressions, what is the recommended depth and rate?
options: Depth 5 to 6 cm at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute
Depth 2 to 3 cm at a rate of 60 compressions per minute
Depth 8 to 10 cm at a rate of 150 compressions per minute
Depth 1 to 2 cm at a rate of 80 compressions per minute
explanation: Press down 5 to 6 cm on an adult's chest at a steady rate of 100 to 120 beats per minute (to the rhythm of 'Stayin' Alive').

q: How should you treat a severe burn at the scene of a road collision?
options: Cool the burn with clean, cold water for at least 20 minutes
Apply butter, ointment, or grease to soothe the skin
Pull away any clothing that has melted onto the burn
Cover with dry cotton wool bandages immediately
explanation: Cool burns immediately with clean cold water for AT LEAST 20 minutes. Never apply oils or creams, and never peel off clothing stuck to the wound.

q: Under what circumstance should you remove an unconscious motorcyclist's crash helmet at the scene of a crash?
options: ONLY if their airway is blocked or they are not breathing and CPR is necessary
Always remove it immediately to cool their head
Whenever they are lying face down
Whenever you suspect a skull fracture
explanation: NEVER remove a motorcycle helmet unless it is essential to clear their airway or perform CPR, as doing so can worsen severe spinal injuries.

q: How far behind your vehicle should a warning triangle be placed on a conventional single carriageway road?
explanation: Place a warning triangle at least 45 metres (147 feet) behind your broken-down vehicle on the same side of the road. WARNING: NEVER use a triangle on a motorway!

q: Why is it strictly prohibited to place a red warning triangle on a MOTORWAY?
options: The danger of walking along the motorway hard shoulder to place it is too great
Wind from passing lorries blows it away
It interferes with radar speed cameras
explanation: High speeds on motorways make walking out to place or retrieve a triangle extremely dangerous. NEVER use a warning triangle on a motorway.

q: What is the very FIRST action you must take if your car stalls and stops directly across railway tracks at a level crossing?
options: Get all passengers out of the car and completely clear of the tracks immediately
Try repeatedly to restart the engine
Use the emergency phone to call the signalman before getting out
Open the bonnet to check the spark plugs
explanation: FIRST: Get everyone out of the vehicle and away from the tracks! SECOND: Use the railway line telephone to alert the signalman. THIRD: Only attempt to move the car if instructed.

q: What does an amber flashing beacon on a slow-moving vehicle (such as a tractor or road sweeper) indicate?
options: A vehicle moving at 25 mph or less
A vehicle carrying dangerous hazardous chemicals
A doctor on an emergency medical call
explanation: Flashing amber beacons warn of slow-moving vehicles travelling at 25 mph or less. They are mandatory for slow vehicles on dual carriageways.

q: If your car catches fire while driving through a road tunnel, what should you do if the vehicle is still driveable?
options: Drive out of the tunnel if possible without causing further danger
Stop immediately and abandon the vehicle in the middle lane
Reverse out of the tunnel in the oncoming lane
Switch on your headlights and accelerate to maximum speed
explanation: If your car catches fire inside a tunnel, try to drive it OUT of the tunnel if it is still operational. If you cannot, pull to the side, switch off engine, and evacuate via emergency exit.

q: What should you do to stop severe arterial bleeding from a deep wound on a casualty's limb?
options: Apply direct, firm pressure over the wound using a clean pad or dressing
Apply a tourniquet around their neck
Wash the wound out with hot soapy water
Remove any glass or knife embedded in the wound
explanation: Apply firm, direct pressure over the wound with a clean pad. If an object is embedded in the wound, DO NOT remove it — apply pressure firmly around the sides of the object.

q: What does a triangular warning sign depicting a tram within a red triangle mean?
options: Trams crossing or sharing the road ahead
Trams have to give way to you
explanation: Trams operate quietly and cannot steer out of their tracks. The triangular sign warns you are approaching a tram crossing or tram route.

q: What do DOUBLE RED lines along the edge of the carriageway (Red Route) signify in London and major cities?
options: Strictly NO STOPPING at any time, even to set down passengers or unload
Free loading zone for goods vehicles
explanation: Double red lines indicate a strict Red Route: NO STOPPING AT ANY TIME for any reason (including dropping off passengers or picking up goods).

q: What does a circular sign with a red ring showing '14′-6″' and '4.4m' with inward-pointing black arrows at the top and bottom indicate?
options: Distance to the next overhead gantry
explanation: Circular signs with a red ring give orders: inward-pointing vertical arrows indicate a mandatory MAXIMUM VEHICLE HEIGHT limit.

q: What is the maximum motorway speed limit for a bus or coach not exceeding 12 metres in overall length?
options: 70 mph (unless fitted with a 62 mph speed limiter)
explanation: Buses and coaches up to 12m length have a maximum motorway speed limit of 70 mph (though speed limiters may restrict them to 62 mph/100 km/h).

q: What is the speed limit within a designated 20 mph zone (indicated by a 20 roundel sign surrounded by traffic calming features)?
options: Advisory 20 mph, legal limit is 30 mph
explanation: A 20 mph zone sign indicates a mandatory 20 mph speed limit, typically accompanied by speed bumps, chicanes, and pedestrian priority.

q: When approaching a School Crossing Patrol displaying a round 'STOP - CHILDREN' sign, what MUST you do?
options: You MUST stop before the sign and wait until the warden has returned completely to the pavement
Slow down to 10 mph and navigate around them
Sound your horn to alert children
Stop only if children are actively on the road
explanation: You MUST stop when signalled to do so by a school crossing patrol. It is an offence to proceed before the patrol has stepped entirely off the carriageway.

q: When passing horses and riders on a public road, what are the two vital Highway Code rules?
options: Pass at NO MORE THAN 10 mph and allow at least 2.0 metres of clearance
Pass at 20 mph and tap your horn lightly
Accelerate past quickly to minimise disturbance
Leave 0.5 metres and rev engine so they know you are there
explanation: Highway Code Rule 215: Pass horses wide and slow. Keep speed to a MAXIMUM of 10 mph and maintain at least 2 metres clearance without sudden revs or horn sounds.

q: What is 'noseweight' in relation to towing a caravan or trailer?
options: The downward vertical force that the trailer's hitch puts onto the vehicle's towball
The weight of the car's front engine and gearbox
The drag created by the caravan's front wind deflector
The weight of the car's front axle when loaded
explanation: Noseweight is the downward load exerted by the trailer hitch onto the towball. Proper noseweight (typically 50-100 kg) is critical to prevent dangerous snaking.

q: When carrying a full load of passengers and heavy luggage in the boot, how should you adjust your tyre pressures?
options: Increase tyre pressures to the manufacturer's recommended 'heavy load' settings
Decrease tyre pressures to improve tyre footprint and grip
Only increase the front tyre pressures
explanation: A heavily loaded car requires increased tyre pressures (specified in the vehicle handbook) to maintain tyre stability, prevent overheating, and ensure correct handling.

q: What is the minimum distance from which you must be able to read a standard UK vehicle registration number plate in good daylight (with glasses or contacts if worn)?
options: 20 metres (66 feet) for new style plates (20.5m for old style)
explanation: You must be able to read a standard post-2001 number plate from a distance of 20 metres (approx. 5 car lengths) in clear daylight.

q: Under what circumstance are you legally exempt from wearing a seatbelt while driving a passenger car?
options: While carrying out a manoeuvre that includes reversing
When driving on a quiet residential road at under 20 mph
When driving a car older than 10 years
explanation: The law provides an exemption from wearing a seatbelt when you are reversing or supervising a learner driver who is reversing, or if you hold a valid medical exemption certificate.

q: What is the legal requirement for windscreen and front side window tinting on vehicles first used after 1 April 1985?
options: Windscreen must let in at least 75% of light; front side windows at least 70%
Any tint is legal as long as headlights are bright
explanation: The windscreen MUST allow at least 75% of light through, and the front side windows MUST allow at least 70% of light through.

q: What should you do before selling a vehicle to ensure you are no longer legally responsible for it?
options: Notify the DVLA immediately online or by sending the V5C/2 slip
Give the entire V5C logbook to the buyer and do nothing else
Post the registration plates to the DVLA
explanation: You MUST notify the DVLA immediately online or send the relevant section of the V5C registration document to the DVLA, otherwise you remain liable for fines and tax.
